DISCLAIMER: I'm a novice with Lean and helping myself A LOT with Claude Code. I try my best to ensure what I send is NOT slop, i.e. I review and edit the code to the best of my abilities and would appreciate feedback.

Hello. I've been trying to prove the algorithmic bounds of Batteries.Data.UnionFind for CSLib as a first contribution.
While doing that I noticed that the invariants asked of the arr argument are rather lax: with those I can't prove the worst case union/find operations to be O(logn) but just O(n), and IIUC I can't prove either the amortized inverse Ackermann (although I used Claude heavily to explain the Tarjan paper to me, so maybe that one can be proved without stronger preconditions).

I believe by enforcing the array to be a result of using constructors (empty, push, link, compress, with compress being needed to track potential mostly) via a witness proof I should be able to prove both. The proof I got for CSLib indeed depends on being able to ensure any root has at least 2^rank elements associated to its set, which the witness is enough to prove for all UnionRank instances (pending deep review of what Claude generated, but superficially it seems correct to me).

Side-effects of the change:

  • Code using UnionFind would need to be adapted to pass the witness proof;
  • Some code guaranteeing only the weaker preconditions might need functional changes, as those would no longer suffice;
  • If the change itself is acceptable, the current invariants would become a consequence of the new one, would it make sense to replace them in the same PR?

Would a PR with this stronger requirement be welcome in Batteries? Are there any other alternatives I may have missed?
Any other suggestions are welcome as well.

Mario Rugiero said:

While doing that I noticed that the invariants asked of the arr argument are rather lax: with those I can't prove the worst case union/find operations to be O(logn) but just O(n), and IIUC I can't prove either the amortized inverse Ackermann (although I used Claude heavily to explain the Tarjan paper to me, so maybe that one can be proved without stronger preconditions).

Make sure you aren't confusing time complexity with amortized time complexity. The normal time-complexity (worst-case) is something like O(m\alpha(m)) for \alpha(m) an inverse Ackermann function. Even if you can't code up and prove this, you should be able to prove O(m loglog m) which would be reasonable in practice. (log(log(10^80))<10, so near constant.)

1. Several answers to this question.
    1a. We don’t have to. Algorithmic theory is only tangentially concerned with the complexity of implementations of algorithms. It is concerned with the asymptotic counting of the number of certain pre specified operations. These can be the operations of the ram model or a bespoke oracle models. Yuval Filmus explained it here
    1b. If you want to recover textbook complexities. You can prove the complexities you assign to basic operations by reducing them to a more basic and well known model. For instance a word ram model.
    1c. It is sometimes simply interesting to ask how many queries are made to an oracle regardless of the cost of this oracle.
    1d. Literature. Let’s say I want to build an algorithm using the latest vertex connectivity algorithm as a procedure. Then I am merely interested in the number of calls to this procedure and its cost. So I make that a query with suitable inputs as many times as my algorithm requires. As long as the previous literature is correct, mine is too. Then you might ask how I verify the literature. As in case 1b, I separately implement that procedure using more basic queries. Repeat until you reach basic models.

  2. Yes. By a suitable choice of underlying query type and a cost model for it, we can formalise algorithms per our preferred approach from 1a, to 1d. The operations you use on arrays can be a query type for example. In fact I have both fan in 2 and unbounded fan in circuits allowing us to define NC and AC complexity classes (including uniform ones since we also have single tape TMs).

  3. Sure.

Just a drive by comment, but the UnionFind algorithm I implemented for Batteries should have all the bells and whistles needed to achieve the inverse ackermann bound, at least using a classical analysis of time complexity. I forget the details but I'm sure you can find them in a CS textbook
